context: Conjecture 1.4 (Hardness of Collision Finding). For fixed constants K ∈ N, κ > 0, and δ > 0, there exists a threshold α⋆ < 1 such that for all α ≥ α⋆ , no polynomial-time algorithm can find a δ-extensive collision with non-negligible probability. We leave confirming this conjecture, or finding algorithmic counterexamples, as an open direction for future work. Paper Organization. The preliminaries fix notation and the formal collision and OGP definitions. Section 4 proves the positive result via a one-sided potential method and a refinement procedure for positive-tail activations. Section 5 proves the first-moment OGP bound for the randomized oscillating activation; the subsequent subsections extend it to correlated-prefix ensembles and derive the online lower bound. 2 Technical Overview The two main technical components of this paper are a positive algorithmic result for positive-tail activations, including the asymmetric binary perceptron (ABP), and a negative online-hardness result via the overlap gap property (OGP) for a randomized activation function. We outline the core ideas behind both directions.

context: 4 Finding Collisions for Positive-Tail Activations We demonstrate that extensive collisions with sufficiently small constant overlap gap can be found at sufficiently low aspect ratios α for activations that are constant on a positive tail. To measure quality, we define the algorithmic rate to be the smaller of the absolute-overlap gap δ, where |⟨x, x′ ⟩| ≤ (1 − δ)n, and the collision ratio α = m/n as n increases. We describe two algorithms. The first one works well in practice, but possibly not so well in theory. We prove its correctness at inverse logarithmic algorithmic rates. We leave open its performance at constant algorithmic rates. We use it as a component in a more complicated algorithm that provably works at fixed positive algorithmic rates, for sufficiently small constants δ and α. The SBP lies between these two regimes. For small κ, it falls within our positive-tail algorithmic window; for very large κ, the activation is nearly constant on typical Gaussian margins, and collisions become trivial. The difficult case is the intermediate window, where the positive-tail escape route no longer applies but no OGP-based hardness result is known for collision finding. Resolving whether SBP is collision resistant in this middle regime, for some α < 1 and some κ, remains a central open challenge.

The difficult case is the intermediate window, where the positive-tail escape route no longer applies but no OGP-based hardness result is known for collision finding. Resolving whether SBP is collision resistant in this middle regime, for some α < 1 and some κ, remains a central open challenge. 1.1 A Statistical Physics Perspective The ABP is susceptible to a second preimage attack: sample y = sign(Ax) for random x and try to solve the so-called teacher-student problem on input (A, y). The output will be an x′ such that, sign(Ax) = y = sign(Ax′ ), which is a collision whenever x′ ̸= x. This occurs with probability at least 1/2 for m < n and with noticeable probability up to α ≤ 1.1. Approximate message passing (AMP) algorithms are known to heuristically solve the teacher-student problem in this regime [1]. Fact 1.1. The ABP is (heuristically) not collision resistant for any α < 1.1.
